templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and are completing {document|a}. It says: "Finish by 4 p.m. Friday. Contact the customer by email. Do not replace any parts without supervisor approval." While working, you find a part that is cracked.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Ask your {lead} to approve replacing the part, and note the crack on {document|the}.
options.why: The document requires supervisor approval before any part is replaced, so getting it first and noting the problem follows it exactly.

options.text: Replace the part right away so the job is finished by 4 p.m. as the document asks.
options.why: The deadline matters, but the document also says not to replace parts without supervisor approval. Both instructions have to be followed.
options.misconception: Meeting the deadline matters more than the other instructions.

options.text: Finish the job with the cracked part and leave it off {document|the}, so nothing delays the deadline.
options.why: Leaving a known problem unreported hides something the supervisor and customer would want to know about.
options.misconception: If the part still works, it is not worth mentioning.

options.text: Call the customer to ask whether you can replace the part, since it is their property.
options.why: The document names the supervisor as the person who approves, and says the customer should be contacted by email.
options.misconception: Anyone connected to the job can give approval.

templates.principle: Read the whole document and follow every instruction in it, including who must approve what.

templates.scenario: You spot several mismatched figures in {document|a} that {coworker} wrote. It goes out later today. You decide to send a short message to {coworker}.
templates.prompt: Which message is the most appropriate?

options.text: Hi {coworker}, I noticed three places where the numbers do not match. Could we check them together before it goes out?
options.why: This message is specific about the problem, polite in tone, and suggests working together before the deadline.

options.text: This document is full of mistakes and has to be completely redone before anyone sees it, so please fix it right now.
options.why: This is harsh and exaggerated, and it does not say where the problems are, which makes them harder to fix.
options.misconception: Blunt criticism is the clearest way to communicate.

options.text: Hey, there might be some issues here or there, so maybe look it over at some point if you get a chance.
options.why: This is so vague that it does not say what the problem is or that the document goes out today.
options.misconception: A gentle hint is more polite than a specific message.

options.text: Yo, this is kinda messed up lol, numbers are off in a few spots, fix it when you can.
options.why: Slang and joking can sound careless in a work message, and it does not mention the deadline.
options.misconception: Casual wording keeps the conversation friendly.

templates.principle: Write to your audience: be specific about the problem, keep a respectful tone, and mention what matters, such as deadlines.

review.notes: Message options are all realistic workplace phrasings.

templates.scenario: {coworker} sends this message to the team.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that is not clear enough.

segments.text: The delivery arrives tomorrow at 9:00 a.m.
segments.whyFine: This line gives a specific day and time.

segments.text: Please put the boxes away in the right spot soon.
segments.why: "Right spot" and "soon" do not say where or by when, so readers have to guess.

templates.principle: Clear instructions name the place, the action and the time instead of words like 'soon' or 'right spot'.

templates.scenario: You need to send your {lead} an email about a schedule change at {workplace|the}.
templates.prompt: Put these writing steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Decide the main point you need to communicate
Write the email with a clear subject line and short sentences

precedence.why: Knowing the main point keeps the message focused.
You can only proofread a message that has been written.
Sending before proofreading means mistakes reach the reader.

templates.principle: Write with purpose: decide your point, write clearly, proofread, then send.

templates.scenario: {Client|a} sends an upset email to {workplace|the} that mixes a complaint, a question about a deadline, and a request for a refund. You have been asked to reply, and you have only skimmed the first paragraph.

options.text: Read the whole email again and list exactly what the person is asking before you start your reply.
options.why: A message that mixes several points can only be answered fully if you know every question in it. Listing them first keeps your reply complete and clear.

options.text: Start writing a reply as soon as you finish the first paragraph so that it goes out quickly.
options.why: Replying to part of a message can miss the deadline question or the refund request, which creates follow-up emails and more frustration.
options.misconception: A fast reply is better than a complete one.

options.text: Forward the email to your {lead} without reading it carefully, so someone else can deal with it.
options.why: You were asked to reply. Passing it along unread adds delay and gives your {lead} no summary.
options.misconception: Passing it on is the safest response.

options.text: Reply to the loudest complaint and assume the other questions will be answered along the way.
options.why: Questions about deadlines and refunds will not be answered unless you address them. Readers expect each point to be covered.
options.misconception: Answering the most emotional part covers everything.

templates.principle: Read a document fully and list what it asks for before you write your response.
templates.timing: Reading and listing the asks comes before drafting.
